paras: The killing of Lafayette Sims was the shooting of a Black lodger by New Orleans police early on February 20, 1903, after a siege of several hours at a Rampart Street boarding house. Police set his room on fire and shot him as he came out. The Associated Press story ran nationwide; Southern papers likened it to the Robert Charles riot of 1900, while a Mississippi editorial and the Black St. Paul Appeal questioned the police.

Sims had a seven-bed room in a Black-run boarding house on South Rampart Street. When the landlord asked him early that morning to unlock it for another lodger, he refused, and the landlord sent for the police. A French-language Louisiana weekly said instead that Sims would not share the room with "toutes sortes de nègres" [all sorts of Negroes].

Police smashed a hole in the door and Sims fired through it; according to the wire, he shot a pistol and a lantern from Officer Windstein's hands, though one Louisiana paper said he shot the officer "through the hand." More police surrounded the house, and when the landlord and an officer pleaded with him, Sims answered, "I'll shoot if you don't go away. I am not going to leave here. They'll burn me in oil. They'll fry me."

An overnight dispatch reported more than fifty police and a crowd of several thousand around the block, and said Chief Journee waited for daylight hoping to avoid "a repetition of the Charles riot of 1900." Journee then had the fire department called, and police threw burning balls of cotton soaked in oil and sulphur into the room. Nearly suffocated, Sims came to the door, where Patrolman Fred Smith shot him and other officers fired at once. Two separate dispatches said seven bullets struck him, one adding that "an officer was the first to fire." The body was driven through a crowd of Black onlookers to the police station and the morgue.

The crowd, put at several thousand by the wire and five hundred by the Beatrice Daily Express, made no demonstration. No report of an inquest or of charges against any officer appears in the coverage. A Hattiesburg editorial claimed an investigation found the man "guilty of no crime known to the police or any citizen," which no other paper reported.

The AP account ran on February 20 and 21 from New York and Minneapolis to Butte, calling Sims "a desperate negro" and the origin of the trouble "trivial." Most papers printed it without comment, under headlines from "Smoked Out and Shot" to a racial slur in the San Antonio Daily Light.

Some Northern headlines hinted at doubt: the Rock Island Argus called it an "Apparently Insane Whim," the Daily Kennebec Journal a "Horrible Fate" that "May Have Been Right," and the Topeka State Journal an "Exhibition of Favorite Southern Pastime" for Mardi Gras visitors. Southern papers invoked Charles instead, the Americus Times-Recorder calling it "Almost a Repetition of the Charles Tragedies." Le Meschacébé called Sims an "émule de Robert Charles" [imitator of Robert Charles], repeated a rumor that he had murdered his wife, and wrote that "heureusement" [fortunately] an officer shot him in the head. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, under "Silly Negro Slain," instead mocked the police, who it said were "wondering why they acted so foolish."

The only Black-press comment found, in the St. Paul Appeal's editorial column on February 28, called Sims an "alleged Afro-American desperado." Where the wire told the story as police work against a desperate man, the Appeal wrote that if authorities pursued "the murderous lynchers" as determinedly, "they would soon, put a stop to them as they did to Simms."

Nearly every detail comes from the police side through the AP. Papers placed the house on South Rampart, North Rampart, or Rampart near Julia Street, and armed Sims variously with a Winchester, a revolver in each hand, or a pistol and the officer's captured revolver. The Hattiesburg editorial, which names no one, said he was a frightened, half-witted man who had run from a policeman, unlike every New Orleans dispatch, which traced the trouble to the landlord.

reader.title: Killing of Lafayette Sims
bases: Sims was shot dead by New Orleans policemen, led by Patrolman Fred Smith, after police besieged his room and had it set on fire; no mob took part in the killing (A12, A13, A9).

The Associated Press story (A1, A12) is matched on the core facts by separate dispatches to the Beatrice Daily Express and Spokane Press (A9, A10), the Record-Herald overnight dispatch (A5, A22) and a Louisiana weekly (A28, A29); the Hattiesburg editorial (A23) disputes Sims's guilt, not the killing.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire (police version)
accounts.gist: Sims locked his seven-bed room, refused the landlord, shot a pistol and lantern from Officer Windstein's hands, held off fifty police for hours, was smoked out with burning cotton, oil and sulphur, and was shot by Patrolman Fred Smith and others.

accounts.label: Chicago Record-Herald overnight dispatch
accounts.gist: During the night a crowd of several thousand and over fifty police surrounded the house; the man had a Winchester and pistols; Chief Journee put off the attack until daylight to avoid a repeat of the Charles riot.

accounts.label: Beatrice and Spokane special dispatches
accounts.gist: Sims appeared pistol in hand and fell with seven bullets in him; the Beatrice dispatch said an officer was reported to have fired first and put the crowd at five hundred.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg Daily Progress editorial
accounts.gist: A half-witted man ran from a policeman out of fright and barred a door; fifty police smoked him out and shot him; an investigation found he had committed no crime.

accounts.label: Le Meschacébé (French)
accounts.gist: An 'émule de Robert Charles' who would not share his room with other lodgers, reputedly a wife-murderer from St. Jean-Baptiste, was shot in the head by an officer before he could kill anyone.

accounts.label: St. Paul Appeal editorial
accounts.gist: An 'alleged' desperado was burned out and shot; the same determination used against lynchers would stop them.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the AP text calling Sims 'a desperate negro' and the origin of the trouble 'trivial', under headlines such as 'Smoked Out and Shot' and 'His Room a Fort'.
Northern headlines hinted at doubt or irony: 'Apparently Insane Whim Results in a Tragedy', 'May Have Been Right, But It's a Queer Story', 'Favorite Southern Pastime'.

Some papers mocked or condemned Sims: a slur headline in San Antonio, 'Made Him a Corpse' in Paducah, 'allowed himself to be killed' in Yorkville, and 'A Negro Tough Smoked Out' and 'émule de Robert Charles' in Le Meschacébé.
The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, under 'Silly Negro Slain', ridiculed the police as having acted foolishly against an innocent, half-witted man.
The St. Paul Appeal called him an 'alleged' desperado and contrasted the police's determination with inaction against lynchers.

info: Early morning of Friday, February 20, 1903, after a siege that began the previous night
A Black-run boarding house on South Rampart street, New Orleans (other versions: North Rampart street; Rampart near Julia street; 'near the new basin')
Lafayette Sims (also spelled Simms; 'Lafayette' in the New York Sun), described as a 'negro' lodger

No crime was charged in the wire account; the trouble began when he refused to unlock his room for the landlord, then fired on police. He was called 'a desperate negro'; one Louisiana paper repeated a rumor that he had killed his wife; a Mississippi editorial said he was innocent of any crime.
